# Independent proof and audit of the concave strip inequality

The candidate proof in `candidate 4ded4943ded696b8`, Sections
1–4, passes an independent audit. This note states the original functional
inequality directly, includes arbitrary interval and endpoint conventions,
and records the complete argument and independently checked algebra.

## Theorem

For any interval \(I\subset[0,1]\) and any nonnegative concave function
\(w:I\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(w(y)\le3-y\),
\[
 \int_I\left[w(y)-3\min\{1-y,\max(w(y)-1,0)\}\right]dy\le1. \tag{1}
\]
The constant is attained by \(I=[0,1]\), \(w\equiv1\), and also by
\(I=[0,1]\), \(w(y)=3-y\).

## Endpoint reduction

An empty or zero-length interval contributes zero. Otherwise write its
closure as \([a,b]\), with \(a<b\). A bounded concave function has finite
one-sided endpoint limits. For example, secant slopes between a fixed
interior point and a point approaching an endpoint are monotone and
bounded, which proves existence of the corresponding function limit.
The limits are nonnegative and satisfy the same affine upper bound.
Defining the two endpoint values to be those limits preserves concavity
by passing to limits in its defining inequality. It changes no integral,
regardless of whether the original interval was open or closed or had
smaller endpoint values. We may therefore assume \(I=[a,b]\) and \(w\)
continuous there.

## Integral decomposition

Define \(w=0\) off \([a,b]\) for integration only, and let \(u=w-1\).
The extended function need not be concave. Write
\[
 V=\int_0^1(-u)_+\,dy,\qquad
 U=\int_0^1u_+\,dy,\qquad
 A=\int_0^1(u+y-1)_+\,dy.
\]
Because
\(\min(1-y,u_+)=u_+-(u+y-1)_+\), the left side of (1) equals
\[
 1-V-2U+3A.
\]
It suffices to prove \(F:=-2U+3A\le V\). If \(A=0\), this is immediate.
Henceforth suppose \(A>0\).

On the original interval, \(u+y-1\) is concave. Its strictly positive
set is an interval with endpoints \(t<r\), where
\(a\le t<r\le b\le1\). Endpoint membership does not affect integrals.
On this active interval the integrand of \(F\) is
\(u-3+3y\); elsewhere it is \(-2u_+\le0\).

If \(t=a\), use \(u\le2-y\) to obtain
\[
 F\le\int_a^r(2y-1)\,dy
   \le\max\left(0,\int_a^1(2y-1)\,dy\right)
   =a(1-a)\le a\le V.
\]
The middle inequality follows by maximizing the convex primitive over
\(r\in[a,1]\); the last holds because the projection is missing on
\([0,a)\). This covers the first endpoint case completely.

## Concavity bounds for the remaining case

Suppose \(t>a\). Continuity gives \(u(t)=1-t>0\). Let \(c\) be the left
endpoint of the nonnegative superlevel interval of \(u\). Then
\(a\le c<t\), \(u(c)\ge0\), and \(u(c)=0\) if \(c>a\). Put
\[
 B=1-c>0,\quad L=t-c>0,\quad
 m=\frac{1-t}{t-c}>0.
\]
Thus \(L=B/(m+1)\).

Concavity gives
\[
 u(y)\ge m(y-c)\quad(c\le y\le t),\qquad
 u(y)\le m(y-c)\quad(t\le y\le r). \tag{2}
\]
The first follows from the chord joining \((c,u(c))\) to
\((t,1-t)\), since \(u(c)\ge0\). For the second, every secant slope after
\(t\) is at most the slope from \(c\) to \(t\), which is at most \(m\).
This argument is valid when \(c=a\) and \(u(c)>0\) as well.

On \([c,t]\), there is no active cap and (2) bounds its contribution to
\(F\) by \(-mL^2\). On \([t,r]\), the contribution is bounded by
\[
 f(y)=\min\{m(y-c),2-y\}-3+3y.
\]
This is increasing: its two affine branches have slopes \(m+3\) and
two. Its primitive from \(t\) is therefore convex, and its maximum on
\([t,1]\) is at an endpoint. Discarding the remaining nonpositive
contributions yields
\[
 F\le\max(0,F_*),\qquad
 F_*=-mL^2+\int_t^1f(y)\,dy. \tag{3}
\]

The branch intersection is
\[
 y_*=(2+mc)/(m+1)=c+L+L/B>t.
\]
It is at most one precisely when \(mB\ge1\). Direct integration gives
\[
 F_*=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\frac{2cBm-1}{2(m+1)},&mB\ge1,\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{B^2m(m-2)}{2(m+1)},&mB\le1.
 \end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
These values agree at \(mB=1\). Each follows by integrating the affine
function of slope \(m+3\) starting at value \(-2(1-t)\), and changing
to slope two at \(y_*\) when that intersection precedes one.

## The missing area controls both branches

We claim
\[
 V\ge V_0:=\int_0^c\min\{1,m(c-y)\}\,dy
 =\begin{cases}
 mc^2/2,&mc\le1,\\
 c-1/(2m),&mc\ge1.
 \end{cases} \tag{5}
\]
If \(c=a\), the missing projection gives \(V\ge c\ge V_0\). Otherwise
\(u(c)=0\), and concavity gives \(u(y)\le m(y-c)\) on \([a,c]\).
The integrand of \(V\) is therefore at least \(m(c-y)\) there, and it
equals one on \([0,a)\). These pointwise bounds imply (5). No concavity
outside the actual projection is used.

For the first branch of (4), when \(mc\le1\), the exact identity is
\[
 2(m+1)(V_0-F_*)=(mc-1)^2+3mc^2\ge0.
\]
When \(mc\ge1\), the corresponding identity is
\[
 2m(m+1)(V_0-F_*)=2(mc)^2+2mc-1>0.
\]
Both denominators are positive, so \(V\ge\max(0,F_*)\) in this branch.

For the second branch of (4), \(m\le2\) makes \(F_*\le0\), which is
enough. If \(m>2\), then \(mB\le1\) implies
\(mc=m-mB\ge m-1>1\), and hence
\[
 V_0=c-\frac1{2m}>\frac1{2m}.
\]
Since \(B^2m^2\le1\),
\[
 F_*\le\frac{m-2}{2m(m+1)}<\frac1{2m}<V_0.
\]
Thus \(V\ge\max(0,F_*)\) in every case. Equation (3) proves
\(F\le V\), completing (1).

The special endpoint values \(c=0\) are included in (4)-(5). The values
\(B=0\), \(L=0\), or \(m=0\) cannot occur in the remaining branch,
because \(c<t<r\le1\). Thus no division by zero or omitted boundary case
is hidden in the proof.

## Audit scope

This establishes the requested one-dimensional inequality without a
tent/extreme-function classification, approximation by polygons,
uncertified numerics, or a monotonicity assumption under hull filling.
The larger triangle signed-area statement when the centroid lies in the
interior is a separate question and is not asserted by this audit.
